segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Phil.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: And I'm Becca.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Sending emails is a big part of modern work and most people try to write emails politely.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Most, but not all.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Recently, BBC Radio 4 programme All In The Mind asked listeners to tell them what they find rude in emails.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Here, presenter Claudia Hammond and guest Pete Olasoga discuss what listeners had to say.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Rachel in Manchester says what annoys her is people who start their emails with just your name and without a simple greeting like hi.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: She says the unnecessary formality always has the effect of putting her immediately on the defensive.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: We've got an anonymous one here who recently received a single emoji in response to a carefully considered and worded email.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: One listener doesn't like emails which start with just her name because they put her on the defensive.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: The phrase to put someone on the defensive means to do or say something which makes them feel threatened or unsure.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Another listener found it rude when their email was answered with a single emoji.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And I think that would annoy me too.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: These emails are examples of people being uncivil an adjective meaning rude or impolite And just a note the noun that goes with this is incivility In this episode we be hearing more about rude emails at work And as usual we be learning some useful new

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: vocabulary, all of which you can find on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: But first, I have a question for you, Phil. Last year, thousands of US government workers

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: received an email requiring them to justify their job by listing five things they had accomplished

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: that week or resign. But who sent this email? Was it A. Donald Trump, B. J.D. Vance or C. Elon Musk?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Ooh, I don't know. Um, maybe J.D. Vance?

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: We'll find out later in the programme.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: Now, according to some psychologists, rudeness in emails is based on a fight or flight response humans feel when stressed.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: Here, psychologist Dr Emma Russell explains these responses for BBC Radio 4's All In The Mind.

segments.speaker: Dr Emma Russell
segments.text: So a fight response is usually when we try to dominate or belittle other people.

segments.speaker: Dr Emma Russell
segments.text: emails that are hostile in tone and language, or even CCing senior personnel in on the message

segments.speaker: Dr Emma Russell
segments.text: in order to elevate an issue and put someone in their place.

segments.speaker: Dr Emma Russell
segments.text: Then the flight response is when people try to protect themselves by withdrawing or avoiding.

segments.speaker: Dr Emma Russell
segments.text: They won reply Or if they do reply maybe they don answer all of the points in the email They just trying to get it off their plate

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The fight response can make us belittle someone make them feel inferior or unimportant

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: For example, a boss sends a group email in which they give someone else the credit for

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: the work you did.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The boss wants to put you in your place.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: An idiom meaning to show someone that they are less important than they think they are.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: The flight response, meanwhile, can be seen when co-workers ignore your message or give a quick, unhelpful reply.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: Such colleagues want to get work off their plate.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: Another idiom meaning to remove tasks from your own workload and give them to someone else to deal with.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Unfortunately, when stressed and working to a deadline, it's hard to make sure all your emails are polite.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: That's what Emma Russell said when she spoke to BBC Radio 4's All In The Mind.

segments.speaker: Dr Emma Russell
segments.text: Because we're operating in these environments where we are all quite frazzled,

segments.speaker: Dr Emma Russell
segments.text: we are more at risk of engaging in instability.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: We're more likely to be uncivil when we're frazzled.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: An informal adjective describing feeling tired or anxious

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: because you're doing too many things at the same time.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Luckily, there are ways to help.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: If you feel angry when writing an email, pause before you hit send. One day it might save your

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: friendship or even your job OK Becca I going to politely ask you to please reveal the answer to your question

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: Of course Phil I asked you who sent the email requiring workers to justify their employment

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: or resign.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: I said that I thought it might have been J.D. Vance.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: Well, we're not going to fire you, Phil, but you are wrong. The correct answer was Elon Musk.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: OK, let's recap the vocabulary we've learnt,

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: starting with the idiom put someone on the defensive,

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: meaning to make someone feel threatened or unsure.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The adjective uncivil means impolite,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: and we have a similar noun that's incivility.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: To belittle someone means to make them feel inferior or unimportant.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: If you put someone in their place,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: you show them that they're not as important as they think they are.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: To get something off your plate means to give someone else a task or problem instead of dealing with it yourself.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And finally, if you're frazzled, you feel tired or anxious because you're doing too much.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up.

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: If you want to know more about communication at work, check out our series Office English.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: It's on our website along with a quiz and a worksheet for this episode.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And that's bbclearningenglish.com.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: But

segments.speaker: Becca
segments.text: now it's goodbye.

segments.speaker: Becca
